B2-1-0.title: ¿-ing o to + verbo?
B2-1-0.question: ¿Qué palabra va antes del segundo verbo?

branches.if: enjoy, avoid, mind, keep, finish, can’t stand, feel like, consider
branches.example: I feel like going out tonight.

branches.if: Una preposición (on, at, of, for, to en look forward to)
branches.example: I’m looking forward to seeing you.

branches.if: decide, hope, offer, refuse, want, plan
branches.example: She refused to apologise.

branches.use: -ing = acción anterior · to = propósito o deber
branches.example: I stopped to call him. / I stopped calling him.

items.note: La primera: dejé de llamarlo. La segunda: me detuve para llamarlo.
La primera es un recuerdo; la segunda, algo que no debes olvidar hacer.

items.a: I’m looking forward to meeting you.
items.b: I’m looking forward to meet you.

B2-1-1.title: De frase simple a cláusula nominal

steps.label: The problem is that…
steps.change: La cláusula con “that” explica el sujeto.

steps.label: What + be
steps.sentence: **What hurt me was that** nobody apologised.
steps.change: Con “what” al inicio el verbo es singular.

steps.label: The reason… is that…
steps.sentence: **The reason** I’m upset **is that** nobody apologised.

branches.use: The problem / truth / fact is that…
branches.example: The truth is that I miss them.

branches.if: Algo que no se sabe aún
branches.use: The question is what / how / where…
branches.example: The question is where he went.
The question is whether to call her.
What matters is that we stay close.

items.a: The question is where he went.
items.b: The question is where did he go.
items.note: Dentro de la cláusula, orden de afirmación: sin inversión.

items.a: What worries me is the silence.
items.b: What worries me are the silence.
items.note: Con una cláusula con “what” como sujeto, el verbo va en singular.

items.a: The reason is that I was tired.
items.b: The reason is because I was tired.
items.note: Se prefiere “the reason is that”; “because” resulta redundante.

items.example: You should have told me. (You didn’t.)
She was supposed to lock it. (She didn’t.)
We didn’t have to pay. (Probably we didn’t.)
I needn’t have cooked. (I did, but it wasn’t necessary.)
We had to leave early. (We did.)

branches.example: We had to show our passports.
We didn’t have to wear a suit.

branches.if: Lo hiciste, pero no era necesario
branches.example: I needn’t have brought a gift.

branches.if: No se hizo y lo lamentas o lo criticas
branches.example: I should have told the manager.
He was supposed to lock the door.

items.note: La primera: no era necesario. La segunda: fue un error pagar.

items.a: I didn’t have to bring food.
items.note: La primera sugiere que no llevaste; la segunda dice que llevaste sin necesidad.
“Must” no tiene pasado: para obligación pasada usa “had to”.

items.example: It can’t have been the cat.
She might not have seen it.
They could have missed the bus.
They might have taken the wrong turn.
He must have forgotten his keys.

steps.label: Pista
steps.sentence: His coat is still on the chair.

steps.label: Casi seguro
steps.sentence: He **must have left** in a hurry.

steps.label: Posible
steps.sentence: He **might have gone** out for lunch.

steps.label: Descartado
steps.sentence: He **can’t have gone** home — it’s raining.

items.a: He could have missed the bus.
items.b: I could have helped, but nobody asked.
items.note: La primera es una posibilidad sobre el pasado; la segunda, una capacidad que no se usó.
El negativo de “must have” (deducción) es “can’t have”.
“Must of” es un error de escritura: se pronuncia /əv/ pero se escribe “have”.

items.a: The guide who showed us around was brilliant.
items.b: Carlos, who showed us around, was brilliant.
items.note: Sin comas identifica cuál guía; con comas, solo agrega información sobre alguien ya identificado.

items.a: My sister who lives in Lima is a nurse.
items.b: My sister, who lives in Lima, is a nurse.
items.note: Sin comas: tengo varias hermanas. Con comas: tengo una sola.

items.a: The city (that) we visited was cold.
items.b: Bogotá, which we visited, was cold.
items.note: Solo en la definitoria puedes omitir el pronombre o usar “that”.

branches.example: The woman who called is my aunt.
Bogotá, which is in the Andes, is cold.
The street where I grew up has changed.
That was the year when everything changed.
The man whose car was stolen called the police.

steps.label: Dos frases
steps.sentence: The district was lovely. We stayed in it.

steps.label: Informal
steps.sentence: The district **(that) we stayed in** was lovely.

steps.label: Formal
steps.sentence: The district **in which we stayed** was lovely.

steps.label: Con where
steps.sentence: The district **where we stayed** was lovely.

steps.label: + material
steps.change: El material va justo antes del sustantivo.

steps.label: + edad
steps.change: La edad va antes del material.

items.note: El tamaño va antes de la edad.
La opinión va antes del color.
Dos adjetivos del mismo tipo (colores) se unen con “and”.

branches.example: Despite the traffic, we loved it.
Despite the fact that it rained, we went out.
Although it rained, we explored.

branches.if: Una oración nueva, después de punto o punto y coma
branches.use: however / nevertheless / on the other hand
branches.example: It’s expensive; however, it’s worth it.

steps.label: Despite
steps.sentence: **Despite the noise**, the neighbourhood is lively.

steps.label: Although
steps.sentence: **Although it’s noisy**, the neighbourhood is lively.

steps.label: However
steps.sentence: The neighbourhood is noisy. **However**, it’s lively.

items.example: Even though it’s tiny, we love it.
It was risky. Nevertheless, we did it.
